Set free by Jehovah, a chief of the tribe of Benjamin ([1 Chr. 8:25](#1Chr.8.25)).
A Tekoite, one of David’s thirty warriors ([2 Sam. 23:26](#2Sam.23.26)).
An Ithrite, also one of David’s heroes ([2 Sam. 23:38](#2Sam.23.38)).
A Jairite and priest, a royal chaplain ([2 Sam. 20:26](#2Sam.20.26)) or confidential adviser (comp. [2 Sam. 8:18](#2Sam.8.18); [1 Chr. 18:17](#1Chr.18.17)).
Runner; wild ass, one of the antediluvian patriarchs, the father of Mehujael ([Gen. 4:18](#Gen.4.18)), and grandson of Cain.
Citizen, chief of an Edomite tribe in Mount Seir ([Gen. 36:43](#Gen.36.43)).

The only son of Abraham by Sarah. He was the longest lived of the three patriarchs ([Gen. 21:1-3](#Gen.21.1)). He was circumcised when eight days old (4-7); and when he was probably two years old a great feast was held in connection with his being weaned.

The son of Amoz ([Isa. 1:1](#Isa.1.1); [2:1](#Isa.2.1)), who was apparently a man of humble rank. His wife was called “the prophetess” (8:3), either because she was endowed with the prophetic gift, like Deborah ([Judg. 4:4](#Judg.4.4)) and Huldah ([2 Kings 22:14-20](#2Kgs.22.14)), or simply because she was the wife of “the prophet” ([Isa. 38:1](#Isa.38.1)). He had two sons, who bore symbolical names.
Spy, the daughter of Haran and sister of Milcah and Lot ([Gen. 11:29](#Gen.11.29), [31](#Gen.11.31)).

Man of shame or humiliation, the youngest of Saul’s four sons, and the only one who survived him ([2 Sam. 2](#2Sam.2)-4). His name was originally Eshbaal ([1 Chr. 8:33](#1Chr.8.33); [9:39](#1Chr.9.39)). He was about forty years of age when his father and three brothers fell at the battle of Gilboa. …
Leaving, one of Abraham’s sons by Keturah ([Gen. 25:2](#Gen.25.2)).
My seat at Nob, one of the Rephaim, whose spear was three hundred shekels in weight. He was slain by Abishai ([2 Sam. 21:16](#2Sam.21.16), [17](#2Sam.21.17)).

The son of Nethaniah, “of the seed royal” ([Jer. 40:8](#Jer.40.8), [15](#Jer.40.15)). He plotted against Gedaliah, and treacherously put him and others to death. He carried off many captives, “and departed to go over to the Ammonites.”

Abraham’s eldest son, by Hagar the concubine ([Gen. 16:15](#Gen.16.15); [17:23](#Gen.17.23)). He was born at Mamre, when Abraham was eighty-six years of age, eleven years after his arrival in Canaan (16:3; 21:5). At the age of thirteen he was circumcised (17:25). He grew up a true child of the desert, wild and wayward. On the occasion of the weaning of Isaac his rude and wayward spirit broke out in expressions of insult and mockery (21:9, 10); and Sarah, discovering this, said to Abraham, “Expel this slave and her son.” Influenced by a divine admonition, Abraham dismissed Hagar and her son with no more than a skin of water and some bread. The narrative describing this act is one of the most beautiful and touching incidents of patriarchal life ([Gen. 21:14-16](#Gen.21.14)).
Son of Obadiah, and viceroy of Zebulun under David and Solomon ([1 Chr. 27:19](#1Chr.27.19)).
A Gibeonite who joined David at Ziklag, “a hero among the thirty and over the thirty” ([1 Chr. 12:4](#1Chr.12.4)).

One who follows on another’s heels; supplanter, ([Gen. 25:26](#Gen.25.26); [27:36](#Gen.27.36); [Hos. 12:2-4](#Hos.12.2)), the second born of the twin sons of Isaac by Rebekah. He was born probably at Lahai-roi, when his father was fifty-nine and Abraham one hundred and fifty-nine years old. Like his father, he was of a quiet and gentle disposition, and when he grew up followed the life of a shepherd, while his brother Esau became an enterprising hunter. His dealing with Esau, however, showed much mean selfishness and cunning ([Gen. 25:29-34](#Gen.25.29)).

Hired ([Gen. 30:18](#Gen.30.18)). “God hath given me,” said Leah, “my hire (Heb. sekhari)...and she called his name Issachar.” He was Jacob’s ninth son, and was born in Padan-aram (comp. 28:2). He had four sons at the going down into Egypt (46:13; [Num. 26:23](#Num.26.23), [25](#Num.26.25)).

Palm isle, the fourth and youngest son of Aaron ([1 Chr. 6:3](#1Chr.6.3)). He was consecrated to the priesthood along with his brothers ([Ex. 6:23](#Exod.6.23)); and after the death of Nadab and Abihu, he and Eleazar alone discharged the functions of that office ([Lev. 10:6](#Lev.10.6), [12](#Lev.10.12); [Num. 3:4](#Num.3.4)). He and his family occupied the position of common priest till the high priesthood passed into his family in the person of Eli ([1 Kings 2:27](#1Kgs.2.27)), the reasons for which are not recorded.

A native of Gath, a Philistine, who had apparently the command of the six hundred heroes who formed David’s band during his wanderings ([2 Sam. 15:19-22](#2Sam.15.19); comp. [1 Sam. 23:13](#1Sam.23.13); [27:2](#1Sam.27.2); [30:9](#1Sam.30.9), [10](#1Sam.30.10)). He is afterwards with David at Mahanaim, holding in the army equal rank with Joab and Abishai ([2 Sam. 18:2](#2Sam.18.2), [5](#2Sam.18.5), [12](#2Sam.18.12)). He then passes from view.
A Benjamite, one of David’s thirty heroes ([2 Sam. 23:29](#2Sam.23.29)).
Oil, one of the sons of Kohath, and grandson of Levi ([Ex. 6:18](#Exod.6.18), [21](#Exod.6.21); [Num. 16:1](#Num.16.1)).
Heel-catcher, a form of the name Jacob, one of the descendants of Simeon ([1 Chr. 4:36](#1Chr.4.36)).
A wild she-goat, one of the Nethinim, whose descendants returned from the Captivity ([Neh. 7:58](#Neh.7.58)).
Concealer, the second of Esau’s three sons by Aholibamah ([Gen. 36:5](#Gen.36.5), [14](#Gen.36.14)).
Mourner, one of the chief Gadites ([1 Chr. 5:12](#1Chr.5.12)).
Made by God, one of David’s body-guard, the son of Abner ([1 Chr. 27:21](#1Chr.27.21)), called Jasiel in [1 Chr. 11:47](#1Chr.11.47).
The son of Jeremiah, and one of the chief Rechabites ([Jer. 35:3](#Jer.35.3)).
Comforted by Jehovah, a descendant of Merari the Levite ([1 Chr. 24:26](#1Chr.24.26), [27](#1Chr.24.27)).
Comforted by God, a Levitical musician ([1 Chr. 15:18](#1Chr.15.18)).
A stream, a descendant of Cain, and brother of Jubal; “the father of such as dwell in tents and have cattle” ([Gen. 4:20](#Gen.4.20)). This description indicates that he led a wandering life.
The father of Shallum ([2 Kings 15:10](#2Kgs.15.10), [13](#2Kgs.15.13), [14](#2Kgs.15.14)), who usurped the throne of Israel on the death of Zachariah.
A descendant of Judah, of whom it is recorded that “God granted him that which he requested” ([1 Chr. 4:9](#1Chr.4.9), [10](#1Chr.4.10)).

Another king of Hazor, called “the king of Canaan,” who overpowered the Israelites of the north one hundred and sixty years after Joshua’s death, and for twenty years held them in painful subjection. The whole population were paralyzed with fear, and gave way to hopeless despondency ([Judg. 5:6-11](#Judg.5.6)), till Deborah and Barak aroused the national spirit, and gathering together ten thousand men, gained a great and decisive victory over Jabin in the plain of Esdraelon ([Judg. 4:10-16](#Judg.4.10); comp. [Ps. 83:9](#Ps.83.9)). This was the first great victory Israel had gained since the days of Joshua. They never needed to fight another battle with the Canaanites ([Judg. 5:31](#Judg.5.31)).

A king of Hazor, at the time of the entrance of Israel into Canaan ([Josh. 11:1-14](#Josh.11.1)), whose overthrow and that of the northern chief with whom he had entered into a confederacy against Joshua was the crowning act in the conquest of the land (11:21-23; comp. 14:6-15). This great battle, fought at Lake Merom, was the last of Joshua’s battles of which we have any record. Here for the first time the Israelites encountered the iron chariots and horses of the Canaanites.
Mourner, one of the chief Gadite “brothers” in Bashan ([1 Chr. 5:13](#1Chr.5.13)).
The fourth son of Simeon ([Gen. 46:10](#Gen.46.10)), called also Jarib ([1 Chr. 4:24](#1Chr.4.24)).
One of the priests who returned from the Exile ([1 Chr. 9:10](#1Chr.9.10)).
The head of one of the courses (the twenty-first) of priests ([1 Chr. 24:17](#1Chr.24.17)).
The last high priest mentioned in the Old Testament ([Neh. 12:11](#Neh.12.11), [22](#Neh.12.22)), sons of Jonathan.
One of the chiefs who subscribed the covenant ([Neh. 10:21](#Neh.10.21)).
Judge, a Meronothite who assisted in rebuilding the walls of Jerusalem ([Neh. 3:7](#Neh.3.7)).

Mountain-goat, the wife of Heber the Kenite ([Judg. 4:17-22](#Judg.4.17)). When the Canaanites were defeated by Barak, Sisera, the captain of Jabin’s army, fled and sought refuge with the friendly tribe of Heber, beneath the oaks of Zaanaim. As he drew near, Jael invited him to enter her tent. He did so, and as he lay wearied on the floor he fell into a deep sleep. …
A son of Shimei, and grandson of Gershom ([1 Chr. 23:10](#1Chr.23.10)).
One of the sons of Shelomoth, of the family of Kohath ([1 Chr. 24:22](#1Chr.24.22)).
A Levite of the family of Merari, one of the overseers of the repairs of the temple under Josiah ([2 Chr. 34:12](#2Chr.34.12)).
The third son of Hebron ([1 Chr. 23:19](#1Chr.23.19)).
A priest who accompanied the removal of the ark to Jerusalem ([1 Chr. 16:6](#1Chr.16.6)).
The son of Zechariah, a Levite of the family of Asaph ([2 Chr. 20:14-17](#2Chr.20.14)). He encouraged Jehoshaphat against the Moabites and Ammonites.
Grasper, a descendant of Caleb, of the family of Hezron ([1 Chr. 2:47](#1Chr.2.47)).
Allotted by God, the first of the sons of Naphtali ([Gen. 46:24](#Gen.46.24)).
Returner, the son of Meshullam, and father of Adiel ([1 Chr. 9:12](#1Chr.9.12)).
The father of Elhanan, who slew Lahmi, the brother of Goliath ([1 Chr. 20:5](#1Chr.20.5)).
A Benjamite, the father of Mordecai, Esther’s uncle ([Esther 2:5](#Esth.2.5)).

A ruler of the synagogue at Capernaum, whose only daughter Jesus restored to life ([Mark 5:22](#Mark.5.22); [Luke 8:41](#Luke.8.41)). Entering into the chamber of death, accompanied by Peter and James and John and the father and mother of the maiden, he went forward to the bed whereon the corpse lay, and said, Talitha cumi, i.e., “Maid, arise,” and immediately the spirit of the maiden came to her again, and she arose straightway; and “at once to strengthen that life which had come back to her, and to prove that she was indeed no ghost, but had returned to the realities of a mortal existence, he commanded to give her something to eat” ([Mark 5:43](#Mark.5.43)).
Pious, the father of Agur ([Prov. 30:1](#Prov.30.1)). Nothing is known of him.
Chief of the twelfth priestly order ([1 Chr. 24:12](#1Chr.24.12)).
Lodger, the last of the four sons of Ezra, of the tribe of Judah ([1 Chr. 4:17](#1Chr.4.17)).
One of those who opposed Moses in Egypt ([2 Tim. 3:8](#2Tim.3.8)).

The son of Zebedee and Salome; an elder brother of John the apostle. He was one of the twelve. He was by trade a fisherman, in partnership with Peter ([Matt. 20:20](#Matt.20.20); [27:56](#Matt.27.56)). With John and Peter he was present at the transfiguration ([Matt. 17:1](#Matt.17.1); [Mark 9:2](#Mark.9.2)), at the raising of Jairus’s daughter ([Mark 5:37-43](#Mark.5.37)), and in the garden with our Lord (14:33). Because, probably, of their boldness and energy, he and John were called Boanerges, i.e., “sons of thunder.” He was the first martyr among the apostles, having been beheaded by King Herod Agrippa ([Acts 12:1](#Acts.12.1), [2](#Acts.12.2)), A.D. 44. (Comp. [Matt. 4:21](#Matt.4.21); [20:20-23](#Matt.20.20)).

The son of Alphaeus, or Cleopas, “the brother” or near kinsman or cousin of our Lord ([Gal. 1:18](#Gal.1.18), [19](#Gal.1.19)), called James “the Less,” or “the Little,” probably because he was of low stature. He is mentioned along with the other apostles ([Matt. 10:3](#Matt.10.3); [Mark 3:18](#Mark.3.18); [Luke 6:15](#Luke.6.15)). He had a separate interview with our Lord after his resurrection ([1 Cor. 15:7](#1Cor.15.7)), and is mentioned as one of the apostles of the circumcision ([Acts 1:13](#Acts.1.13)). He appears to have occupied the position of head of the Church at Jerusalem, where he presided at the council held to consider the case of the Gentiles ([Acts 12:17](#Acts.12.17); [15:13-29](#Acts.15.13): 21:18-24). This James was the author of the epistle which bears his name.

The son of Alphaeus, or Cleopas, “the brother” or near kinsman or cousin of our Lord ([Gal. 1:18](#Gal.1.18), [19](#Gal.1.19)), called James “the Less,” or “the Little,” probably because he was of low stature. He is mentioned along with the other apostles ([Matt. 10:3](#Matt.10.3); [Mark 3:18](#Mark.3.18); [Luke 6:15](#Luke.6.15)). He had a separate interview with our Lord after his resurrection ([1 Cor. 15:7](#1Cor.15.7)), and is mentioned as one of the apostles of the circumcision ([Acts 1:13](#Acts.1.13)). He appears to have occupied the position of head of the Church at Jerusalem, where he presided at the council held to consider the case of the Gentiles ([Acts 12:17](#Acts.12.17); [15:13-29](#Acts.15.13): 21:18-24). This James was the author of the epistle which bears his name.
One of the Egyptians who “withstood Moses” ([2 Tim. 3:8](#2Tim.3.8)).

Wide spreading: “God shall enlarge Japheth” (Heb. Yaphat Elohim le-Yephet, [Gen. 9:27](#Gen.9.27). Some, however, derive the name from yaphah, “to be beautiful;” hence white), one of the sons of Noah, mentioned last in order ([Gen. 5:32](#Gen.5.32); [6:10](#Gen.6.10); [7:13](#Gen.7.13)), perhaps first by birth (10:21; comp. 9:24). He and his wife were two of the eight saved in the ark ([1 Pet. 3:20](#1Pet.3.20)). He was the progenitor of many tribes inhabiting the east of Europe and the north of Asia ([Gen. 10:2-5](#Gen.10.2)). An act of filial piety (9:20-27) was the occasion of Noah’s prophecy of the extension of his posterity.
One of the sons of David ([2 Sam. 5:15](#2Sam.5.15)), born in Jerusalem.

The king of Lachish, who joined in the confederacy against Joshua ([Josh. 10:3](#Josh.10.3)), and was defeated and slain. In one of the Amarna tablets he speaks of himself as king of Gezer. Called also Horam ([Josh. 10:33](#Josh.10.33)).
The fourth antediluvian patriarch in descent from Seth ([Gen. 5:15-20](#Gen.5.15); [Luke 3:37](#Luke.3.37)), the father of Enoch; called Jered in [1 Chr. 1:2](#1Chr.1.2).
One of the chiefs sent by Ezra to bring up the priests to Jerusalem ([Ezra 8:16](#Ezra.8.16)).
Sleeping, called also Hashem ([1 Chr. 11:34](#1Chr.11.34)); a person, several of whose sons were in David’s body-guard ([2 Sam. 23:32](#2Sam.23.32)).

Upright. “The Book of Jasher,” rendered in the LXX. “the Book of the Upright One,” by the Vulgate “the Book of Just Ones,” was probably a kind of national sacred song-book, a collection of songs in praise of the heroes of Israel, a “book of golden deeds,” a national anthology. We have only two specimens from the book, (1) the words of Joshua which he spake to the Lord at the crisis of the battle of Beth-horon ([Josh. 10:12](#Josh.10.12), [13](#Josh.10.13)); and (2) “the Song of the Bow,” that beautiful and touching mournful elegy which David composed on the occasion of the death of Saul and Jonathan ([2 Sam. 1:18-27](#2Sam.1.18)).

Dweller among the people; or to whom the people turn, the Hachmonite ([1 Chr. 11:11](#1Chr.11.11)), one of David’s chief heroes who joined him at Ziklag (12:6). He was the first of the three who broke through the host of the Philistines to fetch water to David from the well of Bethlehem ([2 Sam. 23:13-17](#2Sam.23.13)). He is also called Adino the Eznite (8).
The third of Issachar’s four sons ([1 Chr. 7:1](#1Chr.7.1)); called also Job ([Gen. 46:13](#Gen.46.13)).

He that will cure, the host of Paul and Silas in Thessalonica. The Jews assaulted his house in order to seize Paul, but failing to find him, they dragged Jason before the ruler of the city ([Acts 17:5-9](#Acts.17.5)). He was apparently one of the kinsmen of Paul ([Rom. 16:21](#Rom.16.21)), and accompanied him from Thessalonica to Corinth.

The fourth “son” of Japheth ([Gen. 10:2](#Gen.10.2)), whose descendants settled in Greece, i.e., Ionia, which bears the name of Javan in Hebrew. Alexander the Great is called the “king of Javan” (rendered “Grecia,” [Dan. 8:21](#Dan.8.21); [10:20](#Dan.10.20); comp. 11:2; [Zech. 9:13](#Zech.9.13)). This word was universally used by the nations of the East as the generic name of the Greek race.

The name of the original inhabitants of Jebus, mentioned frequently among the seven nations doomed to destruction ([Gen. 10:16](#Gen.10.16); [15:21](#Gen.15.21); [Ex. 3:8](#Exod.3.8), [17](#Exod.3.17); 13:5, etc.). At the time of the arrival of the Israelites in Palestine they were ruled by Adonizedek ([Josh. 10:1](#Josh.10.1), [23](#Josh.10.23)). They were defeated by Joshua, and their king was slain; but they were not entirely driven out of Jebus till the time of David, who made it the capital of his kingdom instead of Hebron. The site on which the temple was afterwards built belonged to Araunah, a Jebusite, from whom it was purchased by David, who refused to accept it as a free gift ([2 Sam. 24:16-25](#2Sam.24.16); [1 Chr. 21:24](#1Chr.21.24), [25](#1Chr.21.25)).
Able through Jehovah, the wife of King Amaziah, and mother of King Uzziah ([2 Chr. 26:3](#2Chr.26.3)).
A priest in Jerusalem after the Exile ([1 Chr. 9:10](#1Chr.9.10)).
Knowing Jehovah. The chief of one of the courses of the priests ([1 Chr. 24:7](#1Chr.24.7)).
Invoker of Jehovah. The son of Shimri, a chief Simeonite ([1 Chr. 4:37](#1Chr.4.37)).
One of those who repaired the walls of Jerusalem after the return from Babylon ([Neh. 3:10](#Neh.3.10)).
One of the sons of Benjamin, whose descendants numbered 17,200 warriors ([1 Chr. 7:6](#1Chr.7.6), [10](#1Chr.7.10), [11](#1Chr.7.11)).
A Shimrite, one of David’s bodyguard ([1 Chr. 11:45](#1Chr.11.45)). Probably same as in 12:20.
A Korhite of the family of Ebiasaph, and one of the gate-keepers to the temple ([1 Chr. 26:2](#1Chr.26.2)).

A Levite of the family of Merari, one of the leaders of the temple music ([1 Chr. 6:44](#1Chr.6.44); [15:17](#1Chr.15.17), [19](#1Chr.15.19)). He was probably the same as Jeduthun. He is supposed by some to be the same also as (1).
A Levite of the family of Merari ([2 Chr. 29:12](#2Chr.29.12)).
One of the Levitical attendants at the temple, a descendant of Shubael ([1 Chr. 24:20](#1Chr.24.20)).
A Meronothite, herdsman of the asses under David and Solomon ([1 Chr. 27:30](#1Chr.27.30)).
One of the Levites “of the second degree,” appointed to conduct the music on the occasion of the ark’s being removed to Jerusalem ([1 Chr. 15:18](#1Chr.15.18), [20](#1Chr.15.20)).
A Hachmonite, a tutor in the family of David toward the close of his reign ([1 Chr. 27:32](#1Chr.27.32)).
The second of Jehoshaphat’s six sons ([2 Chr. 21:2](#2Chr.21.2)).
One of the Levites of the family of Heman who assisted Hezekiah in his work of reformation ([2 Chr. 29:14](#2Chr.29.14)).
A “prince” and “ruler of the house of God” who contributed liberally to the renewal of the temple sacrifices under Josiah ([2 Chr. 35:8](#2Chr.35.8)).
Jehovah strengthens, one of the chiefs of Ephraim ([2 Chr. 28:12](#2Chr.28.12)).
Jehovah his ornament, the wife of King Jehoash, and mother of King Amaziah ([2 Kings 14:2](#2Kgs.14.2)).

The son and successor of Jehu, king of Israel ([2 Kings 10:35](#2Kgs.10.35)). He reigned seventeen years, and followed the evil ways of the house of Jeroboam. The Syrians, under Hazael and Benhadad, prevailed over him, but were at length driven out of the land by his son Jehoash (13:1-9, 25).

A son of king Josiah ([1 Chr. 3:15](#1Chr.3.15); [Jer. 22:11](#Jer.22.11)), who was elected to succeed his father on the throne, although he was two years younger than his brother Eliakim. He assumed the crown under the name of Jehoahaz (q.v.). He did not imitate the example of his father ([2 Kings 23:32](#2Kgs.23.32)), but was “a young lion, and it learned to catch the prey; it devoured men” ([Ezek. 19:3](#Ezek.19.3)). His policy was anti-Egyptian therefore. Necho, at that time at Riblah, sent an army against Jerusalem, which at once yielded, and Jehoahaz was carried captive to the Egyptian camp, Eliakim being appointed king in his stead. He remained a captive in Egypt till his death, and was the first king of Judah that died in exile.
A Korhite, the head of one of the divisions of the temple porters ([1 Chr. 26:3](#1Chr.26.3)).

Succeeded his father Jehoiakin (B.C. 599) when only eight years of age, and reigned for one hundred days ([2 Chr. 36:9](#2Chr.36.9)). He is also called Jeconiah ([Jer. 24:1](#Jer.24.1); [27:20](#Jer.27.20), etc.), and Coniah (22:24; 37:1). He was succeeded by his uncle, Mattaniah = Zedekiah (q.v.). He was the last direct heir to the Jewish crown. …

The high priest at the time of Athaliah’s usurpation of the throne of Judah. He married Jehosheba, or Jehoshabeath, the daughter of king Jehoram ([2 Chr. 22:11](#2Chr.22.11)), and took an active part along with his wife in the preservation and training of Jehoash when Athaliah slew all the royal family of Judah.
The father of Benaiah, who was one of David’s chief warriors ([2 Sam. 8:18](#2Sam.8.18); [20:23](#2Sam.20.23)).
He whom Jehovah has set up, the second son of Josiah, and eighteenth king of Judah, which he ruled over for eleven years (B.C. 610-599). His original name was Eliakim (q.v.).

Jehovah defends, a priest at Jerusalem, head of one of the sacerdotal courses ([1 Chr. 9:10](#1Chr.9.10); [24:7](#1Chr.24.7)). His “course” went up from Babylon after the Exile ([Ezra 2:36-39](#Ezra.2.36); [Neh. 7:39-42](#Neh.7.39)).
One of the stewards of David’s store-houses ([1 Chr. 27:25](#1Chr.27.25)).
A Levite who taught the law to the people of Judah ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8)).

The eldest son and successor of Jehoshaphat, king of Judah. He reigned eight years (B.C. 892-885) alone as king of Judah, having been previously for some years associated with his father ([2 Chr. 21:5](#2Chr.21.5), [20](#2Chr.21.20); [2 Kings 8:16](#2Kgs.8.16)). His wife was Athaliah, the daughter of Ahab and Jezebel. His daughter Jehosheba was married to the high priest Jehoiada. He sank into gross idolatry, and brought upon himself and his kingdom the anger of Jehovah. The Edomites revolted from under his yoke, and the Philistines and the Arabians and Cushites invaded the land, and carried away great spoil, along with Jehoram’s wives and all his children, except Ahaziah. …
A priest sent by Jehoshaphat to instructruct the people in Judah ([2 Chr. 17:8](#2Chr.17.8)).

Jehovah-swearing, the daughter of Jehoram, the king of Israel. She is called Jehoshabeath in [2 Chr. 22:11](#2Chr.22.11). She was the only princess of the royal house who was married to a high priest, Jehoiada ([2 Chr. 22:11](#2Chr.22.11)).

The son and successor of Asa, king of Judah. After fortifying his kingdom against Israel ([2 Chr. 17:1](#2Chr.17.1), [2](#2Chr.17.2)), he set himself to cleanse the land of idolatry ([1 Kings 22:43](#1Kgs.22.43)). In the third year of his reign he sent out priests and Levites over the land to instruct the people in the law ([2 Chr. 17:7-9](#2Chr.17.7)). He enjoyed a great measure of peace and prosperity, the blessing of God resting on the people “in their basket and their store.”
Son of Ahilud, “recorder” or annalist under David and Solomon ([2 Sam. 8:16](#2Sam.8.16)), a state officer of high rank, chancellor or vizier of the kingdom.
The son of Nimshi, and father of Jehu, king of Israel ([2 Kings 9:2](#2Kgs.9.2), [14](#2Kgs.9.14)).
One of the priests who accompanied the removal of the ark to Jerusalem ([1 Chr. 15:24](#1Chr.15.24)).
The son of Shomer, one of the two conspirators who put king Jehoash to death in Millo in Jerusalem ([2 Kings 12:21](#2Kgs.12.21)).
The son of Obed-edom ([1 Chr. 26:4](#1Chr.26.4)), one of the Levite porters.
King of Israel, the son of Jehoshaphat ([2 Kings 9:2](#2Kgs.9.2)), and grandson of Nimshi. The story of his exaltation to the throne is deeply interesting. …

The son of Hanani, a prophet of Judah ([1 Kings 16:1](#1Kgs.16.1), [7](#1Kgs.16.7); [2 Chr. 19:2](#2Chr.19.2); [20:34](#2Chr.20.34)), who pronounced the sentence of God against Baasha, the king of Israel.
The son of Obed, and father of Azariah ([1 Chr. 2:38](#1Chr.2.38)).
One of the Benjamite slingers that joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:3](#1Chr.12.3)).
A Jew, son of Nethaniah. He was sent by the princes to invite Baruch to read Jeremiah’s roll to them ([Jer. 36:14](#Jer.36.14), [21](#Jer.36.21)).
One of the Levites who took part in praising God on the removal of the ark to Jerusalem ([1 Chr. 16:5](#1Chr.16.5)).
[2 Chr. 29:13](#2Chr.29.13). A Levite of the sons of Asaph.
One of the chief Levites, who made an offering for the restoration of the Passover by Josiah ([2 Chr. 35:9](#2Chr.35.9)).
Dove, the eldest of Job’s three daughters born after his time of trial ([Job 42:14](#Job.42.14)).
One of Simeon’s five sons ([1 Chr. 4:24](#1Chr.4.24)), called also Jemuel ([Gen. 46:10](#Gen.46.10)).

Whom God sets free, or the breaker through, a “mighty man of valour” who delivered Israel from the oppression of the Ammonites ([Judg. 11:1-33](#Judg.11.1)), and judged Israel six years (12:7). He has been described as “a wild, daring, Gilead mountaineer, a sort of warrior Elijah.” After forty-five years of comparative quiet Israel again apostatized, and in “process of time the children of Ammon made war against Israel” (11:5). In their distress the elders of Gilead went to fetch Jephthah out of the land of Tob, to which he had fled when driven out wrongfully by his brothers from his father’s inheritance (2), and the people made him their head and captain. …
The father of Caleb, who was Joshua’s companion in exploring Canaan ([Num. 13:6](#Num.13.6)), a Kenezite ([Josh. 14:14](#Josh.14.14)).
One of the descendants of Asher ([1 Chr. 7:38](#1Chr.7.38)).
The son of Hezron, the brother of Caleb ([1 Chr. 2:9](#1Chr.2.9), [25](#1Chr.2.25), [26](#1Chr.2.26), etc.).
The son of Kish, a Levite ([1 Chr. 24:29](#1Chr.24.29)).
A son of Ezra probably ([1 Chr. 4:18](#1Chr.4.18)).

One of the “greater prophets” of the Old Testament, son of Hilkiah (q.v.), a priest of Anathoth ([Jer. 1:1](#Jer.1.1); [32:6](#Jer.32.6)). He was called to the prophetical office when still young (1:6), in the thirteenth year of Josiah (B.C. 628). He left his native place, and went to reside in Jerusalem, where he greatly assisted Josiah in his work of reformation ([2 Kings 23:1-25](#2Kgs.23.1)). The death of this pious king was bewailed by the prophet as a national calamity ([2 Chr. 35:25](#2Chr.35.25)).
The father of Hamutal ([2 Kings 23:31](#2Kgs.23.31)), the wife of Josiah.
One of the chiefs of the tribe of Manasseh on the east of Jordan ([1 Chr. 5:24](#1Chr.5.24)).
A Benjamite slinger who joined David at Ziklag ([1 Chr. 12:4](#1Chr.12.4)).
A Gadite who joined David in the wilderness ([1 Chr. 12:10](#1Chr.12.10)).
A Levitical musician under Heman his father ([1 Chr. 25:4](#1Chr.25.4)).
